name: Perfectionism Test
tagline: Discover how your high standards help you – and where they hurt.
intro: This test explores four sides of perfectionism: the standards you set, how you treat yourself after mistakes, how much you fear failing and how strongly you need to keep things under control. Answer based on how you usually think and act, not how you would like to be. It takes about five minutes and shows where your drive works for you and where it may be costing you energy.
seoTitle: Perfectionism Test – Free online perfectionist check
seoDescription: Are you a perfectionist? Take this 5-minute test on standards, self-criticism, fear of failure and control and get a personal report with practical tips.

high_standards.name: High standards
high_standards.short: How demanding the goals and quality bar you set for yourself are.
high_standards.low: Your answers suggest you take a relaxed, practical approach to quality. You are happy when something works and rarely lose time polishing details. This makes you efficient and less prone to stress. The flip side is that important work may sometimes get less care than it deserves. Try picking one or two tasks a week that really matter and give them an extra review. Asking a colleague or friend what a great result would look like can also help you raise the bar where it counts.
high_standards.mid: You care about doing things well, but you also know when to stop. This balance is healthy: you can deliver solid work without getting stuck on every detail. Under pressure, though, you may tip towards either rushing or over-polishing. A useful habit is to decide upfront how good a task needs to be, for example by labelling it 'must be excellent' or 'good enough is fine'. Then spend your effort accordingly and protect your time for what matters most.
high_standards.high: Your answers point to very high standards. You notice flaws others miss and often want everything to be excellent. This can drive impressive results, but it can also lead to long hours, delays and little satisfaction when goals are reached. Try setting a clear finish line before you start and a time limit for revisions. Practise sharing work at 90 % and notice that the reaction is usually fine. If the pressure you put on yourself is affecting your sleep, mood or relationships, a qualified professional can help you find a healthier balance.

self_criticism.name: Self-criticism
self_criticism.short: How harshly you judge yourself after mistakes or setbacks.
self_criticism.low: You seem to treat yourself with a good dose of kindness. Mistakes do not linger for long, and you can acknowledge what went wrong without beating yourself up. This self-compassion is a strong foundation for learning and resilience. Keep it up by noticing what you did well each day, not just what you would change. Just make sure you still reflect honestly on errors: a short review of what to do differently next time keeps growth going without harshness.
self_criticism.mid: You are sometimes kind to yourself and sometimes quite harsh. On good days you shrug off mistakes, but on stressful days your inner critic may get louder and replay what went wrong. Try to catch that voice and ask: would I say this to a friend? Rephrase the thought in a fairer way. Another helpful habit is ending the day by writing down three things that went well. Over time this trains your attention towards balance instead of only flaws.
self_criticism.high: Your answers suggest a strong inner critic. You may replay mistakes, struggle to feel proud and feel that you are never quite good enough. This can be exhausting and can quietly undermine your confidence and mood. Start by noticing harsh self-talk and naming it ('there is my critic again') rather than believing it. Practise responding as you would to a friend in the same situation. If self-criticism feels constant or is affecting your wellbeing, talking to a qualified professional, such as a psychologist or counsellor, can really help.

fear_of_failure.name: Fear of failure
fear_of_failure.short: How strongly worry about failing or being judged shapes your actions.
fear_of_failure.low: Failure does not seem to scare you much. You are willing to try new things, share unfinished ideas and learn from setbacks. This openness helps you grow and makes it easier to take on challenges. Keep using it, but remain alert to real risks: a quick check of what could go wrong before big decisions is wise. You might also support others who are more anxious by showing that mistakes are a normal part of progress.
fear_of_failure.mid: You feel some fear of failing, especially when the stakes are high or others are watching. Most of the time you still go ahead, but you may hesitate, delay or play it safe at times. Try breaking daunting tasks into small first steps that feel low-risk. It also helps to ask yourself what the realistic worst case is and how you would cope. Often the answer is less dramatic than the fear suggests, which makes it easier to start.
fear_of_failure.high: Your answers suggest that fear of failure plays a big role for you. You may procrastinate, avoid challenges or dread feedback because mistakes feel threatening. This can hold you back from opportunities and keep stress levels high. Practise small 'safe experiments', such as sharing a rough draft with someone you trust, and notice what actually happens. Focus on effort and learning rather than outcome alone. If worry about failing often affects your sleep, mood or daily life, a qualified professional can help you work through it.

need_for_control.name: Need for control
need_for_control.short: How much you need order, predictability and a firm grip on outcomes.
need_for_control.low: You seem comfortable with uncertainty and happy to let others take the lead. You adapt well when plans change and do not need every detail sorted. This flexibility makes you easy to work with and less prone to stress. The risk is that important details occasionally slip through. A simple to-do list or a short weekly planning moment can give you just enough structure without taking away the spontaneity you enjoy.
need_for_control.mid: You like a certain amount of order and planning, but you can also let go when needed. This is a practical balance: you keep things on track without micromanaging. When stress rises, you may notice yourself checking more or finding it harder to delegate. Try agreeing on clear outcomes with others and then letting them choose the route. Also schedule some unplanned time in your week to practise going with the flow.
need_for_control.high: Your answers suggest a strong need for control. You may prefer to do things yourself, feel tense when plans change and find it hard to trust others with tasks. This can make you reliable, but it can also lead to overload and frustration. Practise delegating one small task fully, without checking it, and see how it goes. Accepting 'different' as not automatically 'worse' frees up energy. If the need for control causes ongoing anxiety or tension in daily life, a qualified professional can help.

summary: Perfectionism is not one trait but a mix of four tendencies. Below you see how you score on each, from 0 to 100 %. High standards can be a real strength, while strong self-criticism, fear of failure or need for control tend to cost energy. This report is based on your own answers and is not a clinical assessment.
